text: A single team can run an informal post-incident discussion and get real value out of it. That stops working once an organization runs dozens of incidents a month across many teams — without a shared format, every postmortem looks different, which makes it nearly impossible to compare incidents, spot repeated causes across unrelated services, or let anyone outside the writing team actually learn from one.

The fix, used by Google's SRE organization and widely adopted since, is a standardized postmortem template every team fills in the same way: a plain-language summary, the impact, a timeline, root cause, what went well, what went poorly, and a table of action items — each one with a named owner and a due date, because an action item with neither isn't really an action item, it's a wish.

Two details matter beyond the obvious fields. Root cause is deliberately plural-friendly, since most real incidents have several contributing factors, and forcing a single cause pressures people to oversimplify. And the timeline is pulled straight from the Scribe's live log — exactly why keeping that log accurate in the moment mattered in the first place.

Above the single-team retro sits a postmortem review board, a recurring cross-team meeting — commonly weekly or biweekly — that asks a different question: what's changing across many postmortems that no single team would notice on its own? It looks for the same root cause recurring on unrelated teams, action items that keep slipping past their due date, and severity trends worth escalating — turning individual incidents into organizational learning instead of isolated lessons that quietly repeat on a different team six months later.

None of this works without blameless language. If an honest timeline risks individual blame, people start writing vaguer timelines and the record stops reflecting what actually happened — which is exactly the record the review board depends on. That closes out incident management. Chapter 3 turns to chaos engineering: finding the gaps before an incident does, instead of after.
